strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations of tool-use agents (error accumulation, API drift, lack of global planning)
Sound bilevel architecture that intuively separates high-level planning from low-level tool execution
Comprehensive technical approach combining structural and behavioral tool dependencies with sophisticated graph learning (HGT, curriculum training, adaptive margins)
Extensive and consistent experimental validation across multiple models (5+ LLMs) and benchmarks showing 12.9-18.7 point TSR improvements over strong baselines
Thorough ablation studies (Table 2) demonstrating contribution of each component (Dynamic+H vs. Static+A)
Detailed implementation details and reproducibility artifacts (inference prompts, training procedures, dataset generation)
weaknesses: Evaluation primarily on simulated APIs rather than real ones (Appendix F.1 with 50 real APIs and 60 queries is limited), limiting claims about real-world robustness to latency, transient failures, rate limiting, and API versioning
No empirical comparison with most closely related work ToolNet (Liu et al., 2024), which also learns tool relations dynamically from logs; claims about ToolNet's limitations are unsubstantiated

Graph construction makes strong assumptions: semantic similarity clustering for parameter unification is underspecified; weight formula (Eq. 4) assumes sufficient historical data and that frequency correlates with utility, both potentially violated in practice
Link prediction quality (76.4% ACC) is moderate but correlation with downstream task performance is not analyzed; no error analysis of which dependency types are predicted poorly

Task generation using random tree structures may not reflect realistic API compositions; Hard tasks defined as only 3+ APIs when real scenarios may have much longer chains with branching and error recovery
Results confounded by supervised fine-tuning: Qwen2.5-14B-SFT achieves 51.3% while Qwen2.5-32B baseline achieves 45.4%, making it unclear how much gain is architectural vs. from fine-tuning
Complex inference prompts (Appendix E.3.1, 20+ pages) may introduce prompt engineering sensitivity; unclear how much of improvement is genuine architectural contribution vs. prompt engineering
Scalability claims lack support: evaluated on pruned subgraphs of 5501 APIs, not full graph; no ablation varying tool set size; graph search limited to depth≤5, hops≤5
Path recombination mechanism (Section 3.3) underexplored: frequency of triggering unknown, no ablation comparing TWNM-guided vs. naive recombination, impact unclear
Missing error analysis: no breakdown of failure modes (wrong API vs. parameter errors vs. token limits); TCR vs. TSR gaps suggest brittleness not addressed; case studies show only successes
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported; some performance differences are small and may not be statistically significant

Incremental novelty in components: HGT is standard, curriculum training with cross-entropy+margin is established practice, graph construction is straightforward; main contribution is combining existing techniques

strengths: Well-motivated problem of scaling LLM agents to large tool ecosystems
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Qwen, DeepSeek, GPT-4o) and datasets (API-Bank, ToolBench) with consistent improvements of 12-19 percentage points
Thoughtful bilevel architecture that cleanly separates task planning from execution via graph-based modeling
Solid ablation studies clearly attributing performance gains to TWNM components
Extensive documentation including detailed prompts, algorithms, and implementation details in appendices
Graph evolution framework with three mechanisms (incremental integration, targeted pruning, edge propagation) shows careful system design
weaknesses: Critical limitation: Primary evaluation is on simulated environments, not real APIs. The paper explicitly states 'As real-time API execution is currently unavailable, evaluation tasks are constructed in a simulated environment'—this fundamentally undermines claims about real-world scalability. Real API dependencies, error modes, and temporal dynamics differ significantly from simulation

Graph component insufficiently validated: Link prediction accuracy is moderate (76.4%); no ablation isolating graph quality's impact on final performance; no empirical validation of graph evolution handling actual API changes

Claimed 'closed-loop optimization' contribution is underdeveloped: Only conceptual illustration (Figure 2); no experiments showing learning from API failures or evidence of actual adaptation to changing APIs over time
Limited real-world validation: Appendix F.1 provides only 60 queries on 50 RapidAPI endpoints—insufficient to support claims about orchestrating 'thousands of tools'

Incomplete baseline comparison: Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-14B (SFT) compared against non-fine-tuned larger models, creating unfair comparison; ToolNet not directly compared; α-UMI is the only strong baseline
Weak statistical rigor: No significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple runs; relies on LLM-based evaluation (GPT-4 for TSR) which lacks human validation and is sensitive to prompt bias

Scalability claims not convincingly supported: Largest evaluation on 5,501 APIs on ToolBench; runtime 30-47 seconds per task (Table 6) suggests potential bottleneck; no computational complexity analysis

Technical details insufficiently justified: Edge weight formula (Eq. 4) uses simple frequency counts; curriculum decay schedule (Eq. 9-10) lacks sensitivity analysis; heuristic search weights (Eq. 19) not ablated
Originality concerns: Bilevel planning, HGT for graphs, and graph-based tool modeling are from prior work; novelty is primarily in engineering integration rather than algorithmic innovation

strengths: Well-motivated bilevel architecture effectively decouples task planning from execution, with a clear four-dimensional decision space covering diverse interaction scenarios
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Qwen, DeepSeek, GPT-4o) and datasets (ToolBench, API-Bank) with thorough ablation studies clearly isolating component contributions
Strong empirical results with consistent 12.9-18.7 point TSR improvements over baselines, particularly robust on hard tasks (+15.4 points on DeepSeek-V3 Hard)
Practical framework addressing real challenges: API drift, dynamic tool updates, and ecosystem evolution through targeted subgraph pruning and incremental node integration
Demonstrates effective knowledge transfer through fine-tuning (14B model matches 32B model performance)
Graph evolution mechanism with three well-designed components (incremental integration, targeted pruning, edge attribute propagation) shows thoughtful engineering
weaknesses: Primary evaluation is simulation-based with LLM-generated synthetic data, masking real-world challenges (latency, rate limiting, authentication, network failures); limited real-world validation (50 APIs, 60 queries) insufficient to validate large-scale claims
Synthetic training data (Appendix D) may introduce systematic biases and artifacts not reflective of actual API call patterns, potentially overfitting to LLM generation artifacts

Graph construction methodology lacks detail: semantic parameter clustering threshold values, false-positive handling not specified; statistical edge weight formula (Eq. 4) oversimplified—ignores temporal decay and conditional patterns; link prediction metrics (ACC 76.4%, F1 77.6%) indicate moderate quality

Individual technical components lack novelty: decision agent is standard LLM fine-tuning on 4-class classification; TWNM uses off-the-shelf HGT; search algorithms are textbook applications of alpha-beta pruning and simulated annealing

Hyperparameter choices poorly justified: graph evolution parameters (λ, η) lack sensitivity analysis; search algorithm parameters (T₀=200, P=20, d_max=4) are hardcoded without justification; fitness function weights (Eq. 19) appear ad-hoc

Scalability claims not fully supported: graph size (~7.9k nodes) is moderate by modern standards; no runtime breakdown of graph construction vs. search vs. LLM inference; missing experiments on scaling with graph size

Experimental methodology concerns: unclear if baselines use supervised fine-tuning (NaviAgent's SFT advantage confounds architectural comparison); outdated baselines (α-UMI from 2024); no confidence intervals or statistical significance testing; only point estimates reported
No qualitative error analysis: failure modes not discussed, no confusion matrices, no analysis of which tool dependency patterns cause problems
Missing discussions on ethical/security implications (unintended side effects from API composition, privilege escalation risks) and when simpler approaches might suffice

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: scaling LLM agents to large, dynamic tool ecosystems with clear motivation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ToolBench, API-Bank), diverse models (Qwen, DeepSeek, GPT-4o), and real APIs (50 RapidAPI endpoints)
Consistent improvements across all tested settings, with particularly strong results on hard tasks (44.9% vs 26.7% baseline on DeepSeek-V3)
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 3, 4, 11) demonstrating contribution of individual components (bilevel design, graph structure, search strategy)
Practical system design with sensible architectural choices: bilevel separation of planning/execution, four-action decision space covering core scenarios, closed-loop adaptation
Extensive documentation with detailed implementation details (Appendix E), case studies (C), algorithms (B), and theoretical justification (I) supporting reproducibility
Real-world validation beyond simulation, demonstrating applicability on live APIs with maintained performance under dynamic conditions
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines standard techniques (HGT for link prediction, Alpha-Beta search, bilevel planning) without fundamental innovation; improvement over ToolNet (dynamic updates) is incremental

Heavy reliance on simulated API evaluation in primary benchmarks (ToolBench, API-Bank); simulated environments cannot capture real failure modes, latency variability, or parameter incompatibilities; real API testing limited to 50 endpoints

Evaluation methodology concerns: TSR scoring relies on LLM-based comparison without inter-annotator agreement or human validation; baseline implementations unclear; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported

Technical rigor issues: path recombination mechanisms (Section 3.3) described informally with no formalization or frequency analysis; graph evolution parameters (η, λ in Eqs. 13-14) lack ablation studies or sensitivity analysis

Theorem 3.1 provides only modest theoretical contribution: straightforward application of standard KL-projection theory; authors acknowledge it is 'intentionally modest' and doesn't characterize full system dynamics

Incomplete technical specifications: graph construction semantic clustering delegated to Appendix A with minimal detail; fine-tuning data described as 'curated' without clear procedure; inference prompts are complex with many heuristics, making sensitivity unclear

Unjustified design choices: sliding window of 3 observation-action pairs has no ablation; search hyperparameters (α₀=0.4, β₀=0.9, T₀=200) lack justification; four-action space boundaries appear arbitrary
Missing robustness analysis: no study of out-of-domain generalization; unclear behavior with incorrect tool relationships in training; parameter naming variation robustness unexamined
Limited scalability validation: tested on 2-5k tools but no analysis of performance scaling; no characterization of failure modes for complex dependency structures
Incomplete comparisons: recent work (ToolGen) mentioned but not compared; limited comparison with graph-based methods; no retrieval augmentation baselines

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks, models, and real-world APIs with consistent improvements
Thorough ablation studies quantifying contributions of individual components
Real-world validation on 50 live RapidAPI endpoints across 7 domains demonstrates practical applicability
Well-organized paper with detailed implementation details and supplementary experiments in appendices
Strong empirical results, particularly on hard tasks (4.3-18.2 point improvements over strongest baselines)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: bilevel architecture (HuggingGPT, Chameleon, α-UMI), TWNM is standard HGT + link prediction, four-action design lacks principled justification
Overstated scalability claims: evaluates on 5.5K APIs (not exceptional); inference time significant (39.6-61.6s for hard tasks); no runtime comparison vs. baselines

Weak theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.1 is mathematically trivial (KL projection = renormalization); acknowledged to not characterize full TWNM process; no justification for KL-minimality criterion
Graph quality not validated: link prediction metrics reasonable (76.4% ACC) but no ablation showing improved link prediction → better task success; no correlation analysis
Unfair experimental setup: fine-tuning on task-specific data while baselines not fine-tuned; LLM-based evaluation introduces bias; no human evaluation; primarily simulated environments
Heuristic-based design without principled justification: pruning criterion (Eq. 13), edge weight updates (Eq. 14), parameter choices (λ, η, μ₀, γ) lack ablations or sensitivity analysis
Limited failure analysis: no systematic error characterization; unclear when/why method succeeds or fails; no investigation of how graph errors propagate
Missing critical ablations: no oracle graph comparison; no static vs. dynamic graph comparison; no comparison with simpler baselines; architecture choices (2 HGT layers, 8 heads) not justified
Real-world evaluation limited in scope: 50 APIs, 303 queries, specific domains; task complexity modest (3+ calls for 'hard'); unclear generalization to other domains
Incremental contribution over ToolNet (2024b): both use graphs; main difference is construction/search strategy, not fundamental architecture

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real challenges in large-scale tool orchestration for LLM agents
Technically sound bilevel architecture with clear separation of high-level planning and graph-based execution
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple scales: simulated (2k-5k tools), real-world (50 live APIs), multiple models
Consistent improvements especially on complex tasks (4.3-18.2 point TSR gains over strongest baseline on Hard split)
Robustness demonstrated by smaller TSR degradation from Easy to Hard tasks compared to baselines
Thorough ablation studies validating contribution of each component (Table 3-4)
Closed-loop learning mechanism with execution feedback for adaptation to API changes and failures
Extensive reproducibility details including inference prompts, training procedures, and maintenance overhead analysis
Practical recovery mechanisms (I/O substitution, upstream rerouting, subgraph switching) for fault tolerance
Heterogeneous Graph Transformer appropriately selected for modeling tool-parameter dependencies
weaknesses: Link prediction performance (76.4-78.4% accuracy, 0.71-0.75 AUC) is moderate; system performance dependent on graph quality but robustness to prediction errors not analyzed
Graph construction methodology underspecified: parameter standardization via semantic clustering lacks quantitative evaluation; no analysis of clustering quality or parameter collision rates
Theoretical contribution limited: Section 3.4 provides only 'local variational lens' not capturing full TWNM dynamics; Theorem 3.1 is straightforward information projection without novelty
Graph evolution mechanisms lack justification: pruning rule (Eq. 13) design choices unexplained; edge weight update (Eq. 14) uses arbitrary mixing coefficient η without ablation
Evaluation primarily on simulated environments (API-Bank, ToolBench); real-world tests limited to 303 queries across 50 APIs—insufficient to claim robustness under real API dynamics
Missing sensitivity analyses: no ablations on hyperparameters (λ, η, α₀, β₀, T₀); search algorithm parameter selection unexplained
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported despite multiple models/tasks tested
Scalability claims need qualification: tested up to 5k tools; memory requirements and graph search complexity for 10k+ tools not discussed
Limited failure analysis: no discussion of failure modes, error types, or when/why NaviAgent fails; action-level ablations incomplete
Improvements on easier tasks are modest (1-7 points on Easy split), suggesting less impact for simpler queries; gains most pronounced on Hard tasks
